items.prompt: Identify two separate tasks that demonstrate division of labour in an invented bag workshop.
items.canonical_answer: One worker cuts fabric panels; another stitches the seams.
marking_guidance: Feature/example (1): cutting panels. Distinct example (1): stitching seams by a different worker.

items.canonical_answer: Concentrating productive effort on a narrower range of tasks or products.
marking_guidance: Meaning/definition and essential element (1): Concentrating productive effort on a narrower range of tasks or products.

items.prompt: Identify two examples of specialisation at the level of a worker or a business.
items.canonical_answer: A worker concentrating on stitching seams; a firm concentrating on one bag product range.
marking_guidance: Characteristic/example (1): worker has a narrower task. Distinct example (1): business has a narrower product range.

items.canonical_answer: Separating a production process into tasks performed by different workers.
marking_guidance: Meaning/definition and essential element (1): Separating a production process into tasks performed by different workers.

items.prompt: Identify two features of division of labour rather than one person making a whole bag.
items.canonical_answer: The process is separated into stages; different workers perform those stages.
marking_guidance: Characteristic (1): separated stages. Distinction/example (1): allocation of those stages to different workers.

items.prompt: Explain how dividing bag production into tasks can raise output per worker-hour, including the role of coordination.
items.canonical_answer: Workers repeat tasks and gain practice, reducing time or errors. Less switching between operations also saves time. More finished output can then be produced per worker-hour if the stages keep pace; an unbalanced stage can instead become a delay.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): workers repeat narrower tasks. Because/mechanism (1): practice or reduced switching saves time. Consequence (1): more finished output per worker-hour. Condition (1): stages must keep pace to avoid a delay. Total 4.

items.prompt: Explain why an invented bag workshop cannot assume more finished output simply because its fabric-cutting worker works faster while stitching capacity is unchanged.
items.canonical_answer: Cut panels can accumulate at the stitching stage; if stitching is the limiting stage, faster cutting alone does not raise finished output.
marking_guidance: Context (1): cut panels wait for unchanged stitching capacity. Reason/conclusion (1): the limiting stage constrains finished output.

items.prompt: Identify the level of specialisation in each example: one worker concentrates on seams; a district concentrates on food processing.
marking_guidance: Characteristic/example (1): worker is individual level. Distinction (1): district is regional level.

items.prompt: Explain how an individual seam specialist can become more productive through practice, with materials and other stages available.
items.canonical_answer: Repeated seams increase task familiarity, reducing errors and time per sound seam. With the other inputs and stages available, the worker can complete more usable output per hour.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): repeated seam task. Because/mechanism (1): greater familiarity. Intermediate consequence (1): fewer errors or less time per sound seam. Final consequence (1): more usable output per hour under the supplied conditions. Total 4.

items.prompt: Evaluate narrow task specialisation for a worker when demand is stable but the worker has little training beyond that task.
items.canonical_answer: Practice can raise skill and productive performance, making the worker useful in the present job. However, a narrow skill makes adjustment difficult if demand or technology changes, and repetition may reduce motivation. Specialisation is justified while the productive gain is valuable, provided broader training or alternative tasks remain available; without them the adjustment risk deserves greater weight.
marking_guidance: Argument for (2): improved task skill (1), better productive performance in the job (1). Argument against (2): difficulty moving after demand changes (1), repetitive work can reduce motivation (1). Condition (1): access to broader training or alternative tasks. Judgement (2): accept productive focus under stable demand (1), conditional on maintaining adaptability (1). Total 7.

items.prompt: Explain how several food processors locating in an invented district can benefit from regional specialisation when suppliers and transport links are reliable.
items.canonical_answer: Concentrated processors create demand for specialised packaging and repair services. Suppliers and skilled workers can serve several firms locally, reducing the time or difficulty of obtaining suitable inputs and improving productive performance.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): related processors concentrate. Because/mechanism (1): demand supports specialised local suppliers/skills. Intermediate consequence (1): suitable inputs/services easier to obtain. Final consequence (1): production improves with reliable links. Total 4.

items.prompt: Evaluate regional specialisation in food processing where specialised suppliers are available but the district has few alternative employers and product demand is volatile.
items.canonical_answer: Shared suppliers and skills can improve productive performance and reduce difficulty obtaining inputs. Against this, falling demand can affect several employers and suppliers together, leaving workers few local alternatives. Specialisation is preferable only if the productive gains justify that concentrated risk and credible adjustment opportunities exist; volatile demand and limited alternatives strengthen the case for some diversification.
marking_guidance: Argument for (2): local specialised suppliers/skills (1), improved access to productive inputs (1). Argument against (2): common demand shock affects several firms (1), workers have few alternatives (1). Condition (1): gains and credible adjustment opportunities relative to volatility. Judgement (2): conditional support (1), diversification receives greater weight under stated risk (1). Total 7.

items.prompt: Explain how a hypothetical southern African economy specialising in fish processing can obtain other goods, assuming overseas buyers and reliable trade links.
items.canonical_answer: Resources concentrate on the chosen productive activity, producing output for sale abroad. Export receipts finance imports, allowing the economy to obtain some goods it does not produce itself.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): resources concentrate in processing. Because/mechanism (1): output is sold to overseas buyers. Intermediate consequence (1): export receipts obtained. Final consequence (1): receipts finance imports under reliable trading conditions. Total 4.

items.prompt: Evaluate national specialisation in one export product where production is well suited to local resources but overseas demand can change sharply.
items.canonical_answer: Productive focus can use local resources effectively and exports can finance a wider range of imports. However, a fall in overseas demand can reduce jobs and export receipts together, restricting imports. National specialisation is worthwhile if productive gains outweigh the vulnerability and the economy can adjust; a narrow volatile export base strengthens the case for diversifying some output.
marking_guidance: Argument for (2): effective use of suited resources (1), export earnings finance imports (1). Argument against (2): demand decline threatens jobs (1), reduced receipts constrain imports (1). Condition (1): productive gains and adjustment capacity relative to volatility. Judgement (2): conditional support for specialisation (1), some diversification justified under concentrated risk (1). Total 7.

items.prompt: Define specialisation (2). Identify two divided tasks in an invented bag workshop where separate workers cut panels and stitch seams (2). Explain one reason division of labour can raise productivity when the stages keep pace (2). Identify the specialisation level for a food-processing district and for a country concentrating on one export range (2).
items.canonical_answer: Specialisation concentrates effort on a narrower range of tasks or products. Cutting and stitching are divided tasks. Repeated practice can reduce time per sound item, raising output per worker-hour with coordinated stages. The district represents regional specialisation and the country national specialisation.
marking_guidance: Meaning (2): concentration of productive effort (1), narrower range of tasks/products (1). Separate points for identification (2): cutting (1), stitching (1). Explanation (2): practice reduces time/errors (1), more usable output per worker-hour (1). Final identifications (2): regional (1), national (1). Marks allocation 8.

items.prompt: Invented teaching data: Orange Sand Bag Workshop divides cutting, stitching and finishing between different workers. With material quality and functioning equipment unchanged, finished sound bags rise from 80 to 100 using the same 20 worker-hours. Its district has specialised packaging suppliers, but most employers depend on a single product market. Describe three features of specialisation in this case (6). Explain mechanisms that could account for the productivity gain and a risk from coordination (7). Discuss whether further regional specialisation is justified if demand for the product becomes volatile and few alternative jobs exist (7).
items.canonical_answer: The workshop separates stages among workers, workers concentrate on narrower tasks, and the district concentrates related activities and suppliers. Repeated practice can reduce mistakes and time per task, while less switching saves time. These mechanisms can increase sound output from the same hours, but one delayed stage can restrict finished production. Regional suppliers and skills can support firms, yet a common demand decline threatens several employers and their workers together. Further concentration is justified only if gains outweigh volatility and credible adjustment options exist; limited alternatives strengthen the case for some diversification.
marking_guidance: Context/data description (6): separate stages (1), allocated to different workers (1); narrower task focus (1), illustrated by cutting/stitching (1); regional activity concentration (1), supported by packaging suppliers (1). Mechanism/explanation (7): repetition (1), learning/fewer mistakes (1), less switching (1), less time per usable output (1), same hours can yield more sound bags (1), stage delay can propagate (1), finished output depends on coordination (1). Both sides/judgement (7): local suppliers support firms (1), shared skills can improve production (1); common demand fall affects employers (1), workers have few alternatives (1); condition is gains versus risk/adjustment capacity (1); limit further concentration under the stated volatility (1), with some diversification justified by that condition (1). Marks allocation 6+7+7=20.

items.prompt: Evaluate specialisation in two separate seven-mark plans. Invented Case 1: a worker learns one repeated bag-stitching task, product demand is stable and cross-training is available. Case 2: a district concentrates employment in food processing, demand for the product is volatile and alternative local employment is scarce. Consider productivity gains, dependence, a decisive condition and a judgement in each case.
items.canonical_answer: Case 1: repeated practice and reduced task-switching can raise productive skill, while narrow work can become monotonous or vulnerable to change. Stable demand and cross-training support a conditional case for individual specialisation. Case 2: regional suppliers and shared skills may benefit firms, but a common demand shock can reduce jobs across the district. Volatility and scarce alternatives make further concentration less attractive unless gains and adjustment measures are sufficiently strong.
marking_guidance: Case 1 marks (7): argument for task skill (1), reduced switching improves productive performance (1); argument against monotony (1), vulnerability to a task-demand change (1); condition stable demand plus cross-training (1); judgement supports specialisation (1) because adaptability remains possible (1). Case 2 allocation (7): argument for shared suppliers (1), relevant skills (1); argument against common demand exposure (1), scarce alternatives (1); condition productive gains versus adjustment capacity (1); judgement cautions against further concentration (1) because the stated conditions increase dependence (1). Total 14.
